entries.name: ball lightning
entries.senseHere: A glowing ball seen during thunderstorms, lasting a few seconds, that appears at random and has no accepted explanation.
entries.background: Reports go back centuries, but almost none have been recorded by instruments. Scientists have proposed many competing theories and none has won agreement.

entries.name: François Arago
entries.background: French astronomer and physicist who wrote the 1837 work Sur le tonnerre, in which the term ball lightning was first used for these phenomena.

entries.name: Walther Brand
entries.background: German school official who wrote Der Kugelblitz (1923), the only German-language monograph on ball lightning.

entries.name: Vladimir Lvovich Bychkov
entries.background: Russian physics professor who keeps a database of Russian ball lightning case reports.

entries.name: Stanley Singer
entries.background: Author of the 1971 book The Nature of Ball Lightning, an early major collection of cases and theories.

entries.name: ALDIS
aliases: Austrian lightning detection and information system
entries.background: Austria's network of sensors that records the time, place and strength of lightning strokes.

entries.name: BLIDS
entries.background: A German lightning location network that detects strokes, used here to match ball lightning sightings to lightning.

entries.name: positive lightning
entries.background: A lightning stroke that carries positive charge to the ground. It is much rarer than negative lightning and usually stronger.

entries.name: cloud–ground stroke
entries.background: A lightning discharge that travels between a thundercloud and the ground, as opposed to one staying within or between clouds.

entries.name: Wilhelm von Haidinger
entries.background: Austrian geologist and mineralogist who belonged to the Imperial Academy of Sciences in Vienna. He reported a ball lightning he saw from his window in 1868.

entries.name: Axel D. Wittmann
entries.background: German astrophysicist at the Göttingen university observatory who saw ball lightning as a child in 1951 and worked on its energy.

entries.name: Othniel Charles Marsh
entries.background: American palaeontologist at Yale, known for dinosaur discoveries, who later led the US National Academy of Sciences.

entries.name: Walther Gerlach
entries.background: German experimental physicist. With Otto Stern he performed the 1922 experiment showing that atomic spin takes only certain discrete values in a magnetic field.

entries.name: Roger Clifton Jennison
entries.background: British radio astronomer and later professor of physical electronics. He reported a glowing sphere drifting down the aisle of an airliner in 1963.

entries.name: Pikes Peak
entries.background: A 4302 m summit in Colorado's Rocky Mountains where Harvard College Observatory kept a weather station from 1874 to 1888.

entries.name: Puy de Dôme
entries.background: A 1465 m old volcano in central France with a weather station and observatory on its summit.

entries.name: Mt Sonnblick
entries.background: A 3106 m peak in the Austrian Alps with a summit weather observatory.

entries.name: Georg Wilhelm Richmann
entries.background: Baltic German physicist at the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences. He was killed by lightning in 1753 while experimenting with atmospheric electricity.

entries.name: Jean-Martin Charcot
entries.background: French physician at the Salpêtrière Hospital in Paris, regarded as a founder of modern neurology. Sigmund Freud studied under him.

entries.name: keraunoparalysis
entries.senseHere: Short-lived paralysis and other nerve effects caused by a lightning strike, distinguished from lasting trauma-related illness.

entries.name: Dorstone
entries.background: A 1936 report from Herefordshire, England, of a red-hot ball that fell into a tub of water and made it boil. It is one of the most cited ball lightning cases.

entries.name: Poughquag
entries.background: A 2008 sighting of a blue ball outside a house in Poughquag, New York. Fluorescence measurements on the glass of the porch window were used to estimate the radiation the object gave off.

entries.name: Camp Blanding
entries.background: A military base in Florida where researchers triggered lightning with rockets trailing metal wire and struck many materials.

entries.name: Qinghai spectrum
entries.background: A 2012 video recording of ball lightning in China with spectrum data. Its spectrum showed lines from iron, silicon, nitrogen and oxygen.

entries.name: Mitino
entries.background: A 2015 Moscow district sighting. Three witnesses filmed a glowing object on mobile phones, which allowed its position to be calculated.
